criteria.title: Suitability criteria
criteria.note: Project assumptions, not NASA requirements. They apply to the scenario, the comparison and the planner.

minSunElevation.label: Min. Sun elevation, °
minSunElevation.hint: The Sun counts as lit only above this angle over the terrain horizon. Grazing light gives little power.

minEarthElevation.label: Min. Earth elevation, °
minEarthElevation.hint: The Earth counts as visible only above this angle over the terrain horizon.

minWindowHours.label: Min. continuous window, h
minWindowHours.hint: Periods with both Sun and Earth that are shorter than this are not counted. 0 — count everything.

maxBlackoutHours.label: Max. darkness, h (0 — no limit)
maxBlackoutHours.hint: The longest period without the Sun that the lander survives on its battery. A mission with a longer darkness is not viable. Applies to the scenario and the comparison, not to the planner.

viablePercent.label: “Viable” from, %
viablePercent.hint: Share of the mission with power and communication from which the site is viable.

marginalPercent.label: “Marginal” from, %
marginalPercent.hint: Share of the mission from which the site is marginal; below it the site is not viable.

hints.sunlight: Share of the mission when the Sun is above the local horizon. No sunlight means solar panels produce nothing and the lander gets cold.
hints.earthLink: Share of the mission when Earth is visible from the site, so the lander can talk to Mission Control directly by radio.
hints.window: Share of the mission when there is both sunlight for power and a direct link to Earth. This is the best time to operate.
hints.longestDarkness: The longest continuous stretch without sunlight. The battery has to last that long.
hints.longestCommsGap: The longest continuous stretch when Earth is hidden and there is no direct radio contact.
hints.sunlightDuration: Total time the Sun is above the horizon during the mission.
hints.earthWindow: Total time Earth is visible and a direct radio link is possible.
hints.heatmap: Rows are landing sites, columns are launch dates. A greener cell means more sunlight and radio contact with Earth during the mission.
hints.sunElevation: How high the Sun stands above the horizon. The lower the Sun, the less power flat solar panels give, so near the pole they are mounted vertically. On Earth the noon Sun stands 30–80° high; at the Moon's south pole it barely clears the horizon, only a few degrees.

welcome.title: Welcome to Lunar Landing Navigator
welcome.intro: The app helps you pick a landing site and a date for a Moon mission: where the Sun gives power and Earth stays in radio view.

steps.site: Pick a landing site on the left.
steps.date: Choose the start date and how long the mission lasts.
steps.verdict: Read the verdict: is it a good place, and why.

sources.title: Sources and assumptions
sources.ephemerisText: Positions of the Sun and Earth as seen from the site: azimuth and elevation, no atmosphere and no refraction, JPL DE441 ephemeris, 60-minute step. Source:
sources.terrainText: Horizon profile of 72 points (every 5° of azimuth) built from LOLA (LRO) elevation data. Source:
sources.terrainFlat: LOLA data is not available for this point: a flat horizon is used, so the result is optimistic. Source:
sources.librationText: Libration (the Moon's wobble) is included: Horizons computes the direction from the site to the Earth with the Moon's actual orientation at every moment. So the Earth does not stand still in the sky but traces a loop: up to ~8° left or right and ~7° up or down from its mean position. Near the pole the Earth hangs low over the horizon, and this loop decides whether it clears the mountains. The Moon's curvature is included in the terrain horizon: distant mountains drop below the edge of the sphere.
sources.validationText: At the six Apollo landing sites the Sun matches the NASA ALSJ values within 0.02° and Earth within 0.22°.
sources.assumption: The viable and marginal shares are project assumptions, not NASA requirements.

help.verdict: The result for the chosen site and dates: Viable, Marginal or Not viable. It depends on how much of the mission has both sunlight (for power) and a direct link to Earth at the same time.
help.sky: The sky seen from above. The edge of the circle is the horizon, the center is a higher point (the scale is zoomed in: near the Moon's pole the Sun and Earth stay very low). North is at the top. The yellow dot is the Sun, the blue dot is Earth, the grey area is the mountains on the horizon: nothing behind them can be seen. The dashed line is the path until the body sets.
help.timeline: Three bars over the days of the mission: when the Sun is above the horizon (yellow), when Earth is visible (blue), and when there is both light and a link (green, the best time to operate). The white "Now" mark is the current moment: click the scale to move it.
help.playback: Press Play and the mission time moves forward: the Sun and Earth drift across the sky and the bars and labels update. The slider rewinds the time, the buttons change the speed.
help.panorama: A 360° view all around you. North is at both edges, then east, south and west going around. The higher the dot, the higher the body is above the horizon. The dark shape is mountains and crater rims.
help.temporal: When the mission starts, in universal time (UTC). A lunar day lasts about 29.5 Earth days; the slider moves the date along the lunar cycle, the buttons move it by a day.
help.bestWindows: The best start day is found for every site: the better the result, the more of the mission has both light and a link to Earth. Click a row to open it in detail.
help.skyGlobe: This is a model of the Moon as it would look from space. The red dot is your site. The yellow arrow shows where the Sun is, the blue one where the Earth is. A grey arrow means that body is below the horizon right now and cannot be seen from the site. The bright part of the ball is day, the dark part is night. Drag the ball to turn it.
help.skyTerrain: This is the ground around the site — a 40 by 40 kilometer patch from lunar orbiter laser data. The red dot is the site, the white arrow points north. The yellow disc is the Sun, the blue one the Earth; they are drawn larger than in real life, otherwise you could not see them. A pale disc means the body is behind a mountain right now. The lower the Sun, the longer the shadows; when it is below the horizon it is night. The relief is stretched twice in height. Drag to rotate, scroll to zoom.
help.neighbours: How much the result depends on the exact spot. The table shows the same scenario a few kilometers from the site. The numbers next to the percentages are the difference from the site itself. "Open" makes the point the new site.
